anatomy.intro: Four two-leaf heads display two distinct patterns above the shared potting medium.

parts.function: One two-leaf body represents the probable L. lesliei appearance group.
parts.label: Tan patterned head

parts.function: A second appearance group has more open upper windows.
parts.label: Grey-green head

parts.function: The division between a head's two leaves is the route for renewal and flowering.
parts.label: Fissure

parts.function: Water and whole-pot weights concern this common container, while each head needs inspection.
parts.label: Shared medium

flowers.text: The working species matches suggest yellow blooms from the tan group and white blooms from the grey group. Photographing each flowering head would add a vivid new comparison to the leaf patterns.

growth.note: The leaf stage of each head guides care through this repeating cycle.

stages.text: Compare the current leaf pairs in both appearance groups.
stages.title: Observe each head

stages.text: A new body may develop as the older leaves shrink.
stages.title: Watch replacement

stages.text: Record fresh heads and dried sheaths without assuming simultaneous renewal.
stages.title: Compare renewed growth

habitat.text: Across southern Africa, Lithops grow among quartz, granite, shale and other stony substrates. Their varied patterns echo those surroundings: a useful way to understand the contrast between the tan islands and open olive windows in this planter.

image.alt: Four Lithops heads in a mauve pot: tan and grey groups, a fissure and shared medium.

lookalikes.name: Split rock
lookalikes.text: Pleiospilos nelii has rounder speckled leaves and a deeper cleft than the flatter windowed Lithops heads.

mature.text: Lithops grow slowly and can persist for decades; Wisconsin Extension reports lifespans reaching 40–50 years. Some heads divide during renewal, gradually changing a small planting into a low cluster.

nameStory.text: The name Lithops evokes a stone-like face: the disguise belongs to living leaves rather than a cactus stem.
